article_classification.basis: Deep technical analysis of the GLM-5.3 model architecture and inference serving economics authored by a named SemiAnalysis research team, drawing on their own InferenceX benchmark platform.

claims.statement: At 150 tokens/sec, GB200 costs approximately $0.044 per million total tokens.

claims.statement: GB200 is about 12% lower cost than MI355X ATOM at the 150 tokens/sec target.

claims.quote: a 17.5% throughput advantage versus 11873 total tokens for GB200
claims.statement: GB300 has a 17.5% throughput advantage versus GB200's 11,873 total tokens per second.

claims.quote: GB200 costs $5.92 per million output tokens at a response speed of 150 tokens per second, which is about 11% less than $6.68 for MI355X ATOM
claims.statement: GB200 costs $5.92 per million output tokens at 150 tokens/sec, about 11% less than MI355X ATOM's $6.68.

claims.statement: GB200 p90 TTFT near 150 tps is roughly 14-19 seconds vs about 1.1-1.2 seconds for MI355X ATOM.

claims.statement: With a ten-second TTFT limit, GB300 with Dynamo-TRT-LLM costs $0.0451, about 26% below ATOM's $0.0607.

claims.metric: share of prompt tokens reused from GPU memory
claims.quote: When concurrency increases from 8 to 16 requests, the share of prompt tokens reused from GPU memory falls from 90.3% to 54.8%.
claims.statement: On B200, as concurrency rises from 8 to 16 requests, prompt tokens reused from GPU memory fall from 90.3% to 54.8%.

claims.quote: keeping the overall cache hit rate above 95% at all concurrency levels
claims.statement: Overall cache hit rate stayed above 95% at all concurrency levels on B200.

claims.quote: the top-k selection operation typically requires the full context to be in HBM, so sparse attention doesn’t eliminate the memory capacity bottleneck
claims.statement: Sparse attention does not eliminate the memory capacity bottleneck because top-k selection typically requires the full context in HBM.

claims.quote: Sparse attention reduces KV cache memory and bandwidth requirements at the SDPA operation, but it does not reduce the overall memory capacity usage.
claims.statement: Sparse attention reduces KV cache memory and bandwidth at the SDPA operation but does not reduce overall memory capacity usage.

claims.statement: GLM-5 is a 744B total, 40B active-parameter mixture-of-experts model.

claims.statement: GLM-5's H=64 (half DeepSeek V3.2's query heads) implies it may be designed for different hardware than H800.

claims.quote: ATOM engine processing prefill in chunks across pipeline stages delivered 98% higher total throughput and reduced median TTFT from 28.6 to 8.7 seconds
claims.statement: ATOM chunked prefill across pipeline stages delivered 98% higher total throughput and reduced median TTFT from 28.6 to 8.7 seconds on an 8 MI355X long-context workload.

claims.quote: vLLM keeping the first decoding step on a consistent CUDA graph execution path reduced average TPOT (time per output token) from about 40 ms to 22 ms in an NVFP4 study
claims.statement: A vLLM NVFP4 study reduced average TPOT from about 40 ms to 22 ms by keeping the first decoding step on a consistent CUDA graph path.

claims.quote: Z.ai claims the orchestrator supports 1000 concurrent rollouts when training GLM-5.
claims.statement: Z.ai claims its multi-task rollout orchestrator supports 1000 concurrent rollouts when training GLM-5.

bottom_line_fact.text: The article argues sparse attention reduces KV cache memory and bandwidth at the SDPA operation but does not reduce overall memory capacity usage, because top-k selection requires the full context in HBM, and system optimizations like HiSparse offload KV cache to host DRAM rather than eliminating it.

bottom_line_inference.text: If sparse attention does not shrink memory capacity needs and instead shifts reuse to host DRAM, demand for HBM, DRAM and NAND in AI serving infrastructure is unlikely to be eroded by this efficiency technique, supporting the memory TAM.

disconfirming_observables: Evidence that sparse attention deployments materially cut aggregate HBM/DRAM provisioning per model
Memory suppliers guiding to softer AI inference demand
lower_priority_if: Evidence sparse attention materially reduces aggregate memory provisioning
Shift of KV cache to non-DRAM storage tiers at scale

near_term_view.text: The article provides a September 28 benchmark snapshot showing host-memory reuse rising sharply with concurrency, but draws a structural conclusion about memory TAM rather than a near-term trading view.

hypotheses.next_research_step: Check whether listed memory suppliers (HBM/DRAM/NAND) quantify AI inference memory demand and whether sparse-attention adoption is factored into their TAM guidance.

opposing_explanations.text: Sparse attention reduces KV cache memory and bandwidth at the SDPA operation, which a naive reading could interpret as reducing memory demand and memory TAM.

raise_priority_if: Memory makers cite inference KV-cache offload to host DRAM as a demand driver
Broader adoption of DSA-style models in production serving

source_implication.text: The article frames the question as how sparse attention affects memory TAM including HBM and NAND, and concludes the sparse attention memory profile alone cannot portray KV cache efficiency; system optimizations keep memory capacity in play and shift reuse to host DRAM.

structural_view.text: Efficiency techniques like sparse attention shift where the memory sits (HBM to host DRAM) rather than eliminating capacity needs, so the memory TAM is more resilient than a naive reading of sparse attention would suggest.

hypotheses.title: Sparse attention does not reduce overall AI memory capacity demand

transmission_chain.text: Sparse attention and KV compression reduce per-operation KV cache reads but top-k selection still needs the full context in HBM.
Serving systems offload KV cache from HBM to host DRAM and keep cache hit rates above 95%, sustaining demand for both HBM capacity and host DRAM.
Sustained memory capacity demand would support revenue of HBM/DRAM/NAND suppliers, but the article does not quantify any earnings or revenue effect for listed memory makers.

unknowns: Whether reduced per-operation memory reads eventually translate into lower aggregate memory purchases as techniques mature
Whether listed memory makers' earnings or guidance reflect this dynamic
The magnitude of the net memory TAM effect, which the article does not quantify

bottom_line_fact.text: In SemiAnalysis's InferenceX GLM-5.3 serving benchmark, NVIDIA GB300/GB200 lead on modeled cost at 150 tokens/sec (GB200 ~12% cheaper than MI355X on total tokens), but AMD MI355X ATOM leads at 100 tps and, under a two-second TTFT limit, is about 9% cheaper than B200; GB300 becomes cheapest only when the TTFT limit is relaxed to ten seconds.

bottom_line_inference.text: No vendor has a uniform cost advantage across streaming-speed targets and latency constraints, so competitive positioning between NVIDIA and AMD in inference serving is workload- and constraint-dependent rather than decisively won by one side.

disconfirming_observables: Hyperscalers standardizing on one vendor for GLM-class serving regardless of latency constraint
Changes in assumed GPU hourly costs that remove the flip in cost leadership
lower_priority_if: Benchmark assumptions (GPU hourly cost) shown to be unrepresentative
One vendor demonstrably dominates across all latency targets

near_term_view.text: Using the September 28 AgentX snapshot, the article shows the vendor cost ranking flips with the latency constraint, a current and research-relevant comparison for inference hardware selection.

hypotheses.next_research_step: Investigate whether AMD MI355X's low-TTFT cost advantage and NVIDIA's high-throughput advantage map to actual accelerator procurement mix at hyperscalers serving agentic LLM workloads.

opposing_explanations.text: At a single 150 tps target on total tokens, GB200/GB300 appear to clearly lead on cost, which in isolation would favor NVIDIA.

hypotheses.premise_condition: Which hardware wins on serving cost depends on the chosen streaming-speed target and the time-to-first-token latency constraint applied.
raise_priority_if: Hyperscalers disclose GLM-class or agentic serving hardware mix
AMD or NVIDIA guidance references inference serving cost competitiveness

source_implication.text: The article states that across the three streaming-speed targets neither system has a uniform cost advantage and that GB300's throughput lead is more than offset by its higher assumed hourly cost at the 150 tps target.

structural_view.text: Serving-cost competitiveness between NVIDIA and AMD accelerators is not uniform and depends heavily on interactivity and TTFT constraints, making headline cost-per-token comparisons misleading without the latency context.

hypotheses.title: GB300/GB200 vs AMD MI355X serving-cost leadership depends on latency constraints

transmission_chain.text: GLM-5.3 agentic serving is benchmarked across NVIDIA GB300/GB200 and AMD MI355X using different inference engines and latency targets.
Modeled serving cost per million tokens shifts between vendors with the streaming-speed target and TTFT limit; GB200 ~12% cheaper at 150 tps, MI355X ~13% cheaper at 100 tps.
Relative serving-cost competitiveness could influence accelerator demand and vendor share, but the article does not quantify any effect on NVIDIA's or AMD's earnings.

unknowns: Whether these modeled serving costs translate into realized hardware purchasing decisions and vendor revenue share
Whether the assumed GPU hourly costs reflect actual market pricing
Whether NVIDIA's or AMD's earnings reflect this competitive dynamic
